title: Worst-case sample complexity of trace reconstruction
formal: For every fixed deletion probability \(\delta \in (0,1)\), determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to \infty , N_{\delta}(n)\): the least number of independent deletion traces that permit exact reconstruction of every unknown n-bit string with success probability at least \(2/3\), with no processing-time bound.
definitions: For \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}, a\) deletion trace is generated by independently retaining each input bit with probability \(1- \delta\) and concatenating the retained bits in their original order. Let \(\mu _{x,\delta}\) be its probability distribution on ⋃_\(\{k=0\}^{n}\{0,1\}^{k}\). Different traces use independent deletion masks. The estimator is given \(n, \delta\) and m independent samples from \(\mu _{x,\delta}\); it receives neither deletion positions nor direct access to x. Its output is an element of \(\{0,1\}^{n}\), and success means equality to the entire original string. One estimator for the given n and \(\delta\) must succeed for every x with probability at least \(2/3\) over the traces and any internal randomness. There is no restriction on processing time, storage, description length or computation between observations: this card asks an information-theoretic sample-complexity question. Formally, let \(N_{\delta}(n)\) be the smallest integer m for which such an estimator exists. The requested asymptotic constants may depend on \(\delta\), but not on n or x. The value is finite because a trace of length n reveals the entire string, and this event has positive probability \((1- \delta )^{n}\). The string is adversarially chosen and has no codebook, sparsity, separation, randomness or other structural promise. Traces are ordinary linear subsequences without cyclic shifts.
answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(f_{\delta}(n)\) and, for every fixed \(\delta \in (0,1)\), constants \(0<c_{\delta}\le C_{\delta}<\infty\) such that \(c_{\delta} f_{\delta}(n)\le N_{\delta}(n)\le C_{\delta} f_{\delta}(n)\) for all \(n\ge 2\), allowing finitely many small n to be absorbed into the constants. Prove both the reconstruction guarantee and the worst-case information-theoretic lower bound in Lean. The dependence on n must be determined within constant factors; deciding only whether a polynomial number of traces suffices does not necessarily determine it.
why: A fundamental question about how much information random subsequences preserve: can every string be identified from polynomially many observations despite completely hidden alignment?

importance.reason: A defining worst-case recovery problem for synchronization noise, linking string algorithms, information theory, statistics and complex-analytic methods.

progress.text: Chase proves the \(\Omega (n^{3/2}/\log ^{7} n)\) worst-case sample lower bound; preprint 2019, journal publication 2021.
Chase obtains \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces for arbitrary strings; preprint 2020 and STOC 2021 presentation.
Chen–De–Lee–Servedio establish nearly matching bounds for local statistical-query reconstruction, rather than unrestricted sample access.
Aamand–Liu–Narayanan obtain \(O(n \log  n)\) traces and polynomial time for mildly separated strings at sufficiently small constant deletion probability.
Burudgunte–Valiant–Wang prove an improved roughly \(n^{5}\) lower bound for the distinct circular trace model at ITCS.
Burudgunte–Valiant–Wang prove a quasipolynomial sample upper bound for general linear trace reconstruction, without a quasipolynomial-time general reconstruction algorithm.

status_note: The July 2026 quasipolynomial sample theorem supersedes the saved 2025 general upper frontier but does not give polynomially many traces. The best unrestricted lower bound cited remains polynomial; circular and local-SQ bounds concern different models. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: The target is the sample-complexity function, including its growth if it is polynomial. The older polynomial-sample question is one qualitative consequence of a determination, rather than the entire target.

The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

There is an immediate exponential upper bound: with probability \((1- \delta )^{n} a\) trace suffers no deletions and reveals the entire string. After sufficiently many samples, such a length-n trace appears with high probability. The challenge is to extract the same information from much shorter typical traces without waiting for this rare event. Their lengths are observable, so the no-deletion event is recognizable.

Lower bounds can focus on two carefully selected strings whose trace distributions are extremely close. If even this binary hypothesis test needs many samples, reconstructing an arbitrary string cannot need fewer. Chase gives a lower bound of \(\Omega (n^{3/2}/\log ^{7} n)\) for fixed deletion probability. This is a substantial obstruction to near-linear reconstruction, but it remains polynomial and is therefore consistent with the target.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint proves a quasipolynomial sample upper bound, including every fixed positive retention probability. Its theorem bounds the number of traces by \(\exp (p^{- 7/3}(\log _{2} n)^{c})\) for an absolute constant c, where \(p=1- \delta\). The strategy uses global statistics involving polylogarithmically many trace positions. It improves the upper frontier considerably while still leaving a gap to a fixed polynomial in n.

The same paper explicitly separates sample complexity from running time. Maximum-likelihood reconstruction can reuse these traces while comparing exponentially many candidate strings, whereas distinguishing two supplied candidates can be implemented much faster. The quasipolynomial sample theorem does not provide quasipolynomial time for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string. Since this card imposes no processing-time limit, this distinction does not weaken the sample result.

The change in statistics matters. A local statistical-query procedure learns only approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that model, nearly matching the older subexponential algorithm. Those lower bounds do not apply to unrestricted use of individual traces or to statistics involving widely separated positions. Thus the new global approach does not contradict the local-query barrier.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that \(O(n \log  n)\) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly \(n^{5}\) is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.
